messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Karim's Story

Karim was thirty-eight when his father died, and only then did he understand that he had spent the previous thirty-two years trying to unsee something that had never really left him. He was six years old the first time his mother screamed in a way that made his body understand danger before his mind could name it. His father had come home late, smelling of arak and rage, and what followed was the sound of his mother's voice breaking like glass, the wet crack of impact, the terrible silence that came after. Karim had hidden in the kitchen cupboard—not because he chose to, but because his legs had carried him there without permission. In the darkness, he could hear everything: the shuffle of feet, his mother's pleas, his father's voice low and certain, the way he spoke as though violence were just another language in the house. There were other nights after that, each one carving deeper grooves into his nervous system. By the time he was twelve, his body had learned to read a man's posture the way other children read books.

Now, at forty-one, Karim worked construction—a job that suited him because it was physical and because the noise and motion could drown out the static in his head. But the job had also become a minefield. Last month, a police officer had come to the site to check building permits, and Karim had felt the familiar surge of panic the moment he saw the uniform. His chest had tightened, his palms had gone cold, and he'd found himself studying the officer's face with an intensity that embarrassed him—watching for the micro-expressions that might signal danger, the way his father's jaw would clench before he struck. The officer had said nothing threatening, but Karim's body didn't care. His hands had shaken for an hour afterward, and that night he'd drifted into one of his escapes, losing himself in a fantasy where he was somewhere else entirely, someone different, someone whose hands didn't shake.

The triggers came without warning. When his foreman asked him to talk about taking on a supervisory role—a conversation about the future, about possibility—Karim had felt the old dread creep in. The thought of having authority over other men, of being the one who might have to confront someone, terrified him in a way he couldn't quite articulate. He'd deflected the offer, made an excuse, and within days had fallen into his old pattern: dwelling on how he used to be, before the tremors, before the hypervigilance had become the default mode of his existence. He spent his evenings replaying memories of himself at twenty-five, when he'd felt capable and whole, before he'd understood how fragile that illusion was.

These memories had a strange quality. Some moments from that childhood lived in his mind with photographic precision—the exact angle of his father's shadow on the kitchen wall, the sound of his mother's breath catching, the texture of the cupboard's wooden shelf against his small back. But when he tried to deliberately access the memories, to piece them into a coherent narrative, they scattered like startled birds. Blank spaces opened up where he expected continuity. The harder he reached for them, the more they eluded him, and this fragmentation only deepened his sense that something catastrophic was lodged inside him, half-buried and dangerous.

The threat monitoring had become automatic. Karim studied faces on the job site, in grocery stores, on the street—always searching for the signs that preceded violence. When someone took too long to respond to a simple question, his mind leapt to the worst interpretation: something bad was happening, something was being hidden from him. A delayed text from a friend meant accident, betrayal, abandonment. The physical reactions came with this vigilance: his heart would race, his muscles would tense as though preparing for impact. These bodily sensations would trigger his escape into fantasy, where he could imagine himself somewhere safe, someone untouchable. But the fantasy only worked temporarily. When he returned to ordinary consciousness, the triggers were still there, waiting. A mention of the future would pull him back into threat mode, which would send him spiraling into avoidance of any confrontation that might clarify what was actually happening versus what he feared might happen. The avoidance meant he'd stopped seeing friends who wanted to discuss their lives, their plans. It meant he'd turned down the supervisory role. It meant he was increasingly alone with the loop that had tightened around him over four decades.

What finally brought Karim to therapy was a panic attack on a job site three weeks ago, triggered by nothing more than a police car passing on the street nearby. He'd collapsed in front of his coworkers, and the shame of that moment—the exposure, the confirmation that he wasn't as functional as he'd pretended—had cracked something open. He sat in the therapist's office now, forty-one years old, still six years old, still hiding in the cupboard, still trying to read danger in every face. What he wanted most was to stop being afraid of men in uniforms, to talk about his future without his chest closing up, to trust that confrontation didn't always end in violence. What he feared most was that the tremors and the hypervigilance were permanent, that he would spend the rest of his life half-present, always scanning, always escaping into a world that didn't exist.
